questions.question: The word polymorphism comes from the Greek roots poly and morphe. What is the literal meaning, and what does it describe in Java?
options: Multiple parents - one class inheriting from several superclasses at once
Many names - one behaviour reachable through several different method names
Many forms - the same method call doing different things depending on the object it acts upon
Changing shape - an object switching to a different class while the program runs
questions.explanation: Poly means many and morphe means form: one call, many forms. A Java object never changes its class at run time, and a class has only one direct superclass - the many forms are the different behaviours a single call can produce depending on the object.

questions.question: In discussions of polymorphism, what does binding refer to?
options: Linking a method call to the method body that will run
Connecting a subclass to its superclass with the extends keyword
Storing an object's fields together in one block of memory
Attaching an access modifier to a method declaration
questions.explanation: Binding links a call site to the body that executes for it. Java draws that link at compile time for overloaded methods (early or static binding) and at run time for overridden methods (late or dynamic binding).

questions.question: Which mechanism is an example of compile-time (static) polymorphism in Java?
options: Method overriding
Method overloading
Downcasting with an explicit cast
Dynamic method dispatch
questions.explanation: With overloading, the compiler picks the right method just by looking at the method name and the argument types at the call site, so the call is bound before the program ever runs. Overriding and dynamic dispatch are resolved at run time by the JVM.

questions.question: Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism in Java is achieved through which mechanism?
options: Method overloading within a single class
Declaring methods as static
Method overriding in a subclass
Giving two methods different return types
questions.explanation: When a subclass overrides an inherited method, the JVM decides at run time which body to execute based on the actual object, not the reference type. This is late (dynamic) binding, also called dynamic method dispatch.

questions.question: What exactly makes up a method's signature in Java?
options: The method name and its return type
The method name plus the number, types, and order of its parameters
The access modifier, the return type, and the method name
The method name and the names given to its parameters
questions.explanation: The signature is the name plus the parameter list - how many parameters, of what types, in what order. Return type, modifiers, and parameter names are not part of it, and a class cannot declare two methods with the same signature.

questions.question: Which statement about upcasting is correct?
options: It needs an explicit cast operator and may fail at run time
It converts a superclass reference into a subclass reference
It rebuilds the object as an instance of the superclass
It is performed automatically by Java and is always safe
questions.explanation: Upcasting goes from subclass to superclass, and because every subclass object IS-A superclass instance it can never fail, so no cast syntax is needed. The object itself is unchanged - only the reference type becomes more general.

questions.question: What question does the instanceof operator answer?
options: Whether a reference variable was declared with a particular type
Whether two reference variables point to the same object
Whether a class contains a method with a particular name
Whether the object a reference currently points to really is of a given type
questions.explanation: instanceof examines the actual object at run time and returns true when it is an instance of the named type or one of its subclasses. That makes it the standard guard to run before attempting a downcast.

questions.question: Which two ingredients are required for method overriding?
options: One class containing two methods with the same name but different parameter lists
An inheritance relationship, and a subclass method with the same signature as a superclass method
One class containing two methods with the same name but different return types
An inheritance relationship, and a subclass method with a different signature from the superclass method
questions.explanation: Overriding spans a superclass and a subclass: the subclass re-declares an inherited method with an identical signature and provides its own body. Same name with different parameter lists in one class is overloading, not overriding.

questions.question: Polymorphism is one of the four major principles of object-oriented programming. Which option names the other three?
options: Encapsulation, inheritance, and abstraction
Overloading, overriding, and casting
Compilation, interpretation, and execution
Classes, objects, and packages
questions.explanation: The four pillars of OOP are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. Overloading and overriding are mechanisms that implement polymorphism, not pillars in their own right.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of a method's signature?
options: The order of its parameter types
The number of parameters it takes
The return type
The method name
questions.explanation: A signature is only the name plus the parameter count, types, and order. Because the return type is excluded, two methods that differ only in return type have the same signature and can never be told apart at a call site.

questions.question: Does this class compile?
options: Yes - the return types differ, so the methods are distinct
Yes - the parameter names differ, so the signatures differ
No - both methods have the signature max(int, int), and a class cannot declare the same signature twice
No - a class may only ever contain one method per method name
questions.explanation: Return types and parameter names are not part of the signature, so both declarations are max(int, int) and the compiler rejects the class. A class CAN reuse a method name, but only with different parameter lists - that is overloading.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: It does not compile - there is no fun(char) overload for fun('A')
int, double, double - the char promotes to the larger double type
int, int, int - all three literals are treated as int
int, double, int - the char widens to int, the nearest fit
questions.explanation: fun(5) exactly matches fun(int) and the double literal 5.0 matches fun(double). There is no fun(char), so 'A' widens to the nearest fitting type, and int beats double, so the third call prints int. All three choices are fixed at compile time.

questions.question: What happens when this program runs?
options: It prints Meow - the JVM dispatches on the actual object, a Cat
It prints Some animal sound - the reference type Animal decides
It does not compile - an Animal variable cannot hold a Cat object
It throws ClassCastException when the assignment runs
questions.explanation: Assigning a Cat to an Animal variable is an automatic, safe upcast. The compiler only verifies that Animal has a speak() method; at run time the JVM sees the object is really a Cat and runs Cat's overriding body.

questions.question: What happens with this code?
options: It prints prrrr - the object really is a Cat
Compile error - the reference type Animal has no purr() method
It compiles but throws ClassCastException at run time
It prints Some animal sound - purr() falls back to speak()
questions.explanation: The compiler checks every call against the reference type, and Animal declares no purr(), so the call is rejected at compile time even though the object is genuinely a Cat. The reference type decides which methods MAY be called; the object type only decides which body runs.

questions.question: A variable is declared as Shape s = new Circle(); where Circle extends Shape and overrides its methods. Which statement correctly describes the roles of the two types?
options: Shape, the reference type, fixes which methods may be called; Circle, the object type, determines which overriding body actually runs
Circle fixes which methods may be called; Shape determines which body runs
Both decisions come from Shape, because that is the declared type of the variable
Both decisions come from Circle, because that is the object that was created
questions.explanation: The compiler validates calls against the declared reference type, so only Shape's methods are callable through s. At run time the JVM dispatches each call to the actual object's class, so Circle's overrides are what execute.

questions.question: What happens with this code?
options: Compile error - an Animal reference can never be cast to Cat
It runs fine - the cast converts the Animal object into a Cat
It compiles, then throws ClassCastException at run time
It runs fine, but c is set to null because the cast fails
questions.explanation: The explicit cast satisfies the compiler, because a variable typed Animal could legitimately point to a Cat. At run time the JVM checks the actual object, finds a plain Animal that is not a Cat, and throws ClassCastException. A cast never converts or changes the object.

questions.question: Why does Java perform upcasts automatically but insist on an explicit cast for downcasts?
options: Downcasting is slower, and the cast tells the JVM to optimise the conversion
An upcast can never fail because every subclass object is-a superclass instance, but the compiler cannot prove a downcast will succeed, so the programmer must explicitly accept the risk
The explicit cast instructs the compiler to convert the object into the subclass type
Upcasts are only permitted inside the subclass's own methods, where they are known to be safe
questions.explanation: Subclass-to-superclass conversion is guaranteed by the inheritance contract, so Java does it silently. A superclass reference might point to anything in the hierarchy, so a downcast is a promise the compiler cannot verify - it compiles the cast and the JVM checks the actual object at run time.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: Meow, Roar, Meow - each element dispatches to its own class's override
Some animal sound three times - the array's type is Animal[]
Compile error - an Animal[] cannot hold Cat and Tiger objects at the same time
Meow, Meow, Roar - the elements are grouped by type before the loop runs
questions.explanation: Placing Cats and Tigers into an Animal[] is automatic upcasting, and each object keeps its actual type. On every iteration the JVM dispatches speak() on the element's actual class, so the output follows the array order: Meow, Roar, Meow.

questions.question: A programmer intends to override speak() in a subclass but types the name as speek() and does not use @Override. What is the result?
options: A compile error, because speek does not exist in the superclass
A run-time exception the first time speak() is called on the subclass
The compiler links speek to speak automatically because the names are so similar
It compiles: speek becomes an unrelated new method, and the subclass silently keeps the inherited speak() behaviour
questions.explanation: Without @Override the compiler has no way to know an override was intended, so the misspelt method is accepted as a brand-new method and calls to speak() still run the superclass body - a silent bug. Writing @Override turns exactly this mistake into a compile-time error.

questions.question: Does this compile?
options: Yes - @Override is documentation only and never affects compilation
Yes - speek simply overloads speak, which is legal
No - @Override fails because speek does not override any method from a supertype
No - a subclass may not declare methods that its superclass lacks
questions.explanation: @Override asks the compiler to verify that the method genuinely overrides an inherited one. Animal has no speek(), so compilation fails - exactly the safety net the annotation provides. (speek would not overload speak either: overloads must share one name.)

questions.question: Which option correctly contrasts method overloading with method overriding?
options: Overloading needs an identical signature in a subclass; overriding needs different signatures in one class
Overloading is same name with different signatures in one class, resolved by the compiler; overriding is an identical signature across superclass and subclass, resolved by the JVM at run time
Overloading is resolved at run time by the JVM; overriding is resolved at compile time
Overloading requires an inheritance relationship; overriding requires different parameter lists
questions.explanation: Overloading lives inside one class: one name, several parameter lists, and the compiler picks by the arguments (early binding). Overriding spans an inheritance pair: the same signature gets a new body in the subclass, and the JVM picks by the object's actual type (late binding).

questions.question: Why can the decision about which overriding method body a call like a.speak() should run generally NOT be made at compile time?
options: Overriding methods are stored in separate files that the compiler never reads
The compiler is forbidden from inspecting subclass method bodies
Overridden methods are re-translated to bytecode each time they are called
The actual class of the object that a will refer to may only be known while the program is running
questions.explanation: A reference such as Animal a may end up holding a Dog or a Cat depending on run-time events like user input or random choices. The compiler knows only the reference type, so the body can only be chosen when the actual object is known - at run time.

questions.question: Which overloaded method does the marked call execute?
options: add(int, int) - the compiler always prefers the first declared overload
add(double, double) - both arguments are converted to double first
add(int, double) - the argument types match this signature exactly
None - the call is ambiguous, so the class does not compile
questions.explanation: The compiler resolves an overloaded call by matching the argument types against the available signatures: 5 is an int and 3.5 is a double, so add(int, double) is an exact match and no conversion is needed. The choice is made entirely at compile time.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: Vehicle engine starts, then Car drives
Car engine starts, then Car drives
Car engine starts, then ClassCastException at the (Car) cast
Vehicle engine starts only - the instanceof test is false
questions.explanation: v points to a Car, so dynamic dispatch runs Car's startEngine() even through a Vehicle reference. The instanceof check passes because the object really is a Car, so the guarded downcast succeeds and drive() becomes callable through the Car reference.

questions.question: A method processes an Animal[] by calling speak() on every element. A new subclass Wolf, with its own speak() override, is added later and Wolf objects are put into the array. What must change in the processing method?
options: Nothing - it is written against Animal, and dynamic dispatch will find Wolf's override automatically
A new instanceof branch with a cast to Wolf must be added inside the loop
The parameter must be redeclared as a new array type that mentions Wolf
The method must be rewritten, because existing code always needs modification when subclasses are added
questions.explanation: This is extensibility, a key benefit of polymorphism: code written against a superclass works unchanged for every subclass, including ones written later. Each call still dispatches to the element's actual type at run time.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: Sub - the object is a Sub, so dynamic dispatch selects Sub's method
Nothing - it fails to compile because static methods cannot be redefined in a subclass
Sub, then Base - both versions execute in order
Base - static methods are bound using the reference type at compile time
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, not to any object, so no dynamic dispatch happens: the reference type Base decides at compile time. Sub's identically-named static method hides Base's rather than overriding it.

questions.question: Why do static methods not participate in runtime polymorphism?
options: Static methods always execute faster, so the JVM skips the dispatch step to save time
Static methods are implicitly final and can never be redeclared in a subclass
Dynamic dispatch chooses a body using the actual object's type, and a static method belongs to a class rather than to any object
Static methods can only be called from other static methods, where no objects exist
questions.explanation: Dynamic dispatch answers the question: what object is this call landing on? A static call has no receiver object, so the reference (class) type decides at compile time. A subclass redeclaring the same static method produces hiding, not overriding, and marking it @Override is a compile error.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: true, then true
true, then false
false, then true
false, then false
questions.explanation: instanceof tests the actual object, and the object is a Cat, so a instanceof Cat is true regardless of the Animal reference type. Because every Cat is-an Animal, a instanceof Animal is true as well.

questions.question: What happens at lines A and B?
options: Neither line compiles - elements of an Animal[] are Animals, not Cats
Line A fails at run time; line B succeeds
Both lines succeed - the casts convert each element into a Cat
Line A succeeds; line B compiles but throws ClassCastException because the object is a Tiger
questions.explanation: Both downcasts compile, because an Animal element could plausibly be a Cat. At run time the JVM checks each actual object: zoo[0] really is a Cat, so line A succeeds; zoo[1] is a Tiger, and a Tiger is not a Cat (they are siblings, not parent and child), so line B throws ClassCastException.

questions.question: What does this program print?
options: Car engine, then Vehicle engine - each call follows the variable's declared type
Car engine, then Car engine - both references point to the same Car object
Vehicle engine, then Vehicle engine - the upcast permanently converts the object
Vehicle engine, then Car engine - upcasting reverses the method lookup order
questions.explanation: Upcasting changes only the reference type - the object on the heap is still a Car. Dynamic dispatch looks at the object, not at the variable used to reach it, so both calls run Car's override and print Car engine twice.

questions.question: In an inheritance pair where a subclass redefines a superclass method with the same signature, what are the two methods called?
options: The superclass method is the overridden method; the subclass method is the overriding method
The superclass method is the overriding method; the subclass method is the overridden method
The superclass method is the overloaded method; the subclass method is the overloading method
Both are simply called virtual methods, and the two terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: The superclass supplies the method that gets overridden; the subclass supplies the overriding version that runs when dispatch selects it. Overloading terminology does not apply here, because only one signature is involved.
